passage: Satellites are remarkable tools that orbit our planet to help us in daily life. Unlike airplanes that rely on air to generate lift, rockets use powerful engines to eject fuel, allowing them to travel through the vacuum of space where there is no air to push against. Once a satellite reaches its orbit, it does not need its engines to keep moving; it stays in motion due to its high speed and Earth's gravity, which acts like a tether. Geostationary satellites are special because they orbit at a very high altitude of about 36,000 km, matching Earth's rotation to stay fixed above one specific location. This is very different from the International Space Station, which orbits much closer to Earth. Satellites do much more than just take photographs. They use advanced sensors to monitor crop health, track cyclone movements, and even detect flood-prone areas by analyzing light beyond what our eyes can see. Furthermore, your phone does not receive location data from a single satellite; it calculates your precise position by receiving signals from at least four different GPS satellites simultaneously. These signals travel at the speed of light, but because of the vast distances involved, there is a tiny, measurable delay before they reach your device.

items.evidence: Once a satellite reaches its orbit, it does not need its engines to keep moving; it stays in motion due to its high speed and Earth's gravity, which acts like a tether.
items.q: A satellite switches off its engines after reaching orbit. What happens to it next?
options: It keeps circling, held by speed and gravity
It falls back because its engines stopped
It floats still because space has no gravity
It drifts away since nothing holds it now
items.explain: In orbit, high speed and Earth's gravity keep a satellite moving; engines are not needed.

wrong.why: thinks engines must run all the time
thinks there is no gravity in space
ignores gravity acting like a tether

items.evidence: Geostationary satellites are special because they orbit at a very high altitude of about 36,000 km, matching Earth's rotation to stay fixed above one specific location.
items.q: Why does a geostationary satellite always stay above the same city?
options: It goes round as fast as Earth spins
It is not moving at all in space
It is held still there by Earth's gravity
It flies low, just above that city
items.explain: It matches Earth's rotation, so it keeps pace with the city below and stays above it.

wrong.why: thinks it is not moving at all
thinks gravity pins it in one place
thinks it orbits only a few hundred km up

items.evidence: They use advanced sensors to monitor crop health, track cyclone movements, and even detect flood-prone areas by analyzing light beyond what our eyes can see.
items.q: How can a satellite check crop health that a normal photo cannot show?
options: It reads light that our eyes cannot see
It changes the weather over the crops
It takes a clear photo in daylight
It gets reports from towers on the ground
items.explain: Satellite sensors study light beyond what our eyes see, showing crop health a photo misses.

wrong.why: thinks satellites only use normal cameras
thinks information comes only from ground towers

items.evidence: Furthermore, your phone does not receive location data from a single satellite; it calculates your precise position by receiving signals from at least four different GPS satellites simultaneously.
items.q: Meena's phone shows her exact spot on a map. How does the phone find it?
options: It works it out from four satellites' signals
It gets her position from one satellite
It is tracked by a satellite that reports back
It asks the nearby mobile towers only
items.explain: The phone calculates its own position using signals from at least four GPS satellites together.

wrong.why: thinks one GPS satellite is enough
thinks the satellite tracks the phone
thinks location comes only from towers

items.evidence: These signals travel at the speed of light, but because of the vast distances involved, there is a tiny, measurable delay before they reach your device.
items.q: A GPS signal travels from a satellite to your phone. When does it arrive?
options: It arrives after a tiny, measurable delay
It arrives instantly, with no delay at all
It arrives late because it travels slowly
It arrives only after many minutes
items.explain: Signals move at light speed, but the huge distance causes a tiny, measurable delay.

wrong.why: blames slow speed instead of distance
overestimates the delay, ignoring the word tiny
